title: integer arithmetic, primes, gcd, and modular math
concepts: The greatest common divisor (GCD) is the largest positive integer dividing both inputs; Euclid's algorithm repeatedly replaces (a,b) with (b,a mod b).
The least common multiple can be computed as |a/gcd(a,b) times b|, dividing first to reduce overflow risk and handling zero separately.
Trial division only needs candidates through the square root, while the Sieve of Eratosthenes marks composite multiples in O(n log log n) time for a bounded range.
Prime factorization by repeated division builds exponents of prime factors; precomputed smallest-prime factors accelerate repeated factorizations within a bounded maximum value.
Modular addition and multiplication keep values within a residue class, but intermediate multiplication may overflow before the modulus is applied.
Binary exponentiation computes powers in O(log exponent) multiplications; modular division is multiplication by an inverse and is valid only when that inverse exists.
For prime modulus p, a nonzero residue a has inverse a^(p-2) mod p by Fermat's little theorem; for composite moduli, an inverse exists exactly when gcd(a,m)=1.
Combinatorial formulas using factorials and inverse factorials modulo p require factorial indices below p and a prime modulus; constraints must justify every algebraic shortcut.
